Name: Oslo Court
Description:
Rank: 99

Oslo Court, an absurd cream puff of a restaurant on the ground floor of an International Style housing block in St John’s Wood, is the one place on this list where the food is a bystander to the experience. Some of the truly great restaurants are not about food at all, but about comfort and fantasy. The real draw of Oslo Court is things being precisely as you remember them (if you’re old enough) or the delight of unearned nostalgia. It’s a place where Melba toast comes unbidden, where the most avant-garde main is steak Diane, where at least one table will be celebrating an 80th birthday, and where sides (including genuinely excellent latkes) are technically unlimited. A word of warning: if the legendary septuagenarian dessert waiter Neil Heshmat is on duty, recommending the best dessert on his trolley, which he’s saved just for you, Oslo Court reaches some kind of perfection; if it’s his night off, the whole thing might fall down like a pale pink house of cards.

Name: The Quality Chop House
Description:
Rank: 98

I once heard the legendary French chef Olivier Roellinger say that the template for every great chef must be the image of a mother nourishing a hungry child. Shaun Searley at Quality Chop House is not a nourishing mother: he has the mien of a chef out to kill his customers. My most memorable meal here showcased every known shade of brown plus a few that the restaurant invented: a game broth that tasted like Bovril if you gave it a knighthood; a tranche of brill spine cooked hard to stand up to a glossy Sichuan-ish sauce; grouse (a mahogany breast, a study in brown in its itself) with trimmings; brown bread fried in something unholy; plum jam the colour of sin; a scoop of liver parfait as smooth as chestnut gelato atop dripping toast; gravy. I am only in the mood for this cooking once in a blue moon, but, my god, if you want to feel like a boy being fattened up by a witch in a Brothers Grimm tale, nowhere else will do.

Name: Sonora Taquería
Description:
Rank: 97

There are now plenty of good individual tacos in London: the lengua from Guacamoles, the taco paisa from Comalera, the al pastor from El Pastor. But Sonora is the only London taqueria that passes the ultimate test: would I stake the city’s reputation on bringing the most annoying American person I know? I would relish it. Since being refurbished this spring, Michelle Salazar de la Rocha and Sam Napier’s Stoke Newington restaurant has been operating on a level close to some of the best in New York or LA. The aggressive caramelisation on the carne asada, the sticky, concentrated jus of tongue and head in the cabeza, the translucent, lunar quality of the flour tortillas: all these small touches are reminders that making great tacos is an exercise in miniaturism. The tiniest item on the menu, the bean quesadilla, is a must order, perfectly honouring the tortilla, which is so delicious I would happily call it a roti.

Name: Core
Description:
Rank: 96

When you go to Core, you’ll be asked to choose between two menus: ‘Classics’, which is made up of tried-and-tested dishes, and the more experimental ‘Seasons’. If you go as a pair, you should order both, which will give you a chance to glimpse the light and shadow of Clare Smyth’s three-Michelin-starred cooking. I prefer the heavier Classics menu – particularly how Smyth fashions a silk purse from the sow’s ears of potato, dulse and herring roe, creating something that feels decadent with humble ingredients. But what marks both menus out from the ‘international fine dining’ aesthetic that plagues this genre are a sense of style, limpid and playful, and a strong sense of place, thanks to the focus on British ingredients. If you can’t afford a tasting menu, fear not! You can order Core’s best dish at the bar: an update on the Malteser that solves that chocolate’s central problem – its harshness on the teeth. With a Wonka-like flourish, the kitchen conjures a cloud of malt that sits atop the dessert like a fascinator and dissolves like cotton candy.

Name: Little Nyonya
Description:
Rank: 95

When Kelvin Chan and June Fan reopened their 14-seater cafe Little Nyonya in Sutton in 2023, almost exactly as it was in Quarry Bay 6000 miles away, they invented something new – not a diaspora restaurant, but a whole restaurant in diaspora. Little Nyonya may be the only restaurant in London operating on Hong Kong rules: a cramped kitchen putting out six dishes for around three hours a day, queues round the block, cash only. Its customers, mainly from the new Hongkonger community, aren’t looking for traditional HK comfort food but for what Little Nyonya was famous for back home: its elegant laksa, with broth the colour of virgin sand, either enriched with the marine funk from the heads of three prawns or by the QQ texture of glossy fish balls and homemade fish and pork beancurd rolls. I’ve often had the feeling eating here that, next to the gestalt of Little Nyonya’s laksa, other soup noodles are mere bowls of broth with toppings.

Name: Udaya
Description:
Rank: 94

As East Ham’s Kerala scene spirals, offering statement short rib mandis, fish nirvanas and other hybrids with the food of the Gulf, restaurants like Prajeesh Kumar’s Udaya feel reassuringly old school. This is simple drinking food that comes in three modes – stir-fried, deep-fried or battered to an absolute crisp – designed to pair with beers in the lazy heat of a coastal city. Seafood is a particular strength here, from a crab fry that will have you scraping the shell with your teeth to get as much of the coating as possible, to a platter of devilled squid, mussels and fish that is closer in spirit to popcorn chicken than it is to the seafood platter at Bentley’s. So many of the dishes here are excuses to eat crispy onions with parotta or appam, particularly the full chicken fry, which resembles what might happen if a KFC bargain bucket, a blooming onion and a whole shelf of spices got into a fight.

Name: Café Japan
Description:
Rank: 93

The list of prestigious sushi restaurants that fish wholesaler Atariya supplies has always been its assurance of quality. But most impressive is its own restaurant in Golders Green, where short supply chains means a £48 omakase – something of a London miracle. Make sure to sit at the small wooden counter at the back and chef Shigeru Fukushima, or his deputy, will send across 14 pieces of nigiri in a half-hour businessman’s trip. British fish are prioritised here: turbot, Dover sole animated with yuzu, red mullet, barely charred to emphasise the sweetness of its ruddy skin. Tuna comes four ways: lean early on, fatty at the midway point, medium-fatty at the end and, best of all, chopped finely onto a hot crispy block of rice, so it melts like a sundae from the residual heat. In a city full of high-end omakase and Itsu branches, Café Japan is a rare win for the middle, and the one sushi restaurant I consistently want to return to.

Name: Regency Cafe
Description:
Rank: 92

Every city needs a tourist trap that is legitimately good. New York has Katz’s, Paris has Breizh Café and London has the Regency. You’re now more likely to overhear Americans than black-cab drivers (who have decamped to the Astral, over the road), but the various cycles of Regency hype and recent change of ownership (it is now owned by the Turkish Gungor brothers) have not affected the food, which remains superb. The fry-ups are its trademark – real, fat sausages, eggs like milky glass eyes, slabs of bubble crisped up on the plancha – but what really sets the Regency apart is the care taken on the non-breakfast items. Come early afternoon, after the tourist rush, and a perfect rectilinear pie with braising steak and gravy will be your reward. Meanwhile, the bronzed chips, served with the pie, or with thin slices of cooked ham, or with the Friday fish, are as recognisable a Regency calling card as its green-and-white gingham-patterned tables.

Name: Toklas
Description:
Rank: 91

Art-world-adjacent side project, Italian-ish canteen cooking, thespian diners, balcony by the Thames: it has not escaped me that Toklas is what The River Cafe might be had it not chosen to live out its life in stately isolation over in West London. This is also a testament to Amanda Sharp and Matthew Slotover (of Frieze Art Fair) for fashioning one of the great London dining rooms from a vast, resounding rectangle of concrete, as well as chef Chris Shaw who, since taking over in 2023, has pushed the food in crowd-pleasing directions. Toklas’s culinary lineage is the Cafe itself, combined with the painterly impressionism of Spring, Petersham Nurseries and Sessions Arts Club. It’s evident in the saffron orange of mussels escabeche, the butter yellow of good pasta and emulsified sauce and the seemingly endless supply of primary-coloured Todolí citrus animated from still life to uplift meat, fish and desserts. This is watercolour cuisine at its best.

Name: Master Wei
Description:
Rank: 90

Guirong Wei didn’t need to open Master Wei, having already mainstreamed Shaanxi cuisine at Highbury’s Xi’an Impression, but the name is a statement of intent. We know from experience (see A.Wong) that when a Chinese chef in London puts their own name on a restaurant, they’re no longer messing around. I’m not sure there is a single noodle dish in the city I love eating more than the pork biang biang with tomato and egg, an order for the indecisive that combines the caramel sweetness of the meat and its juices, the textures and acidity of tomato, a coddled cloud of egg and perfectly al dente belt noodles. And yet if there is one, it might just be Master Wei’s cool, polytextural liang pi, which is the noodle equivalent of sticking your head in an ice-cold bath. And these are just the main courses; I like to treat the (under-ordered) salt and pepper squid as dessert.

Name: La Barra
Address: 147 Eagle Yard Arch, Maldonado Walk, SE1 6SP
Description:
Rank: 89

The calling-card of La Barra, a Colombian restaurant under the railway arches at Elephant and Castle, was given to its original owner Maria-Luisa Riascos Solis by one of her chefs: a recipe for pica pollo, the Dominican version of fried chicken. That recipe has followed La Barra through each of its iterations and ownerships, the one Dominican dish on a Colombian restaurant’s menu – a passing of the baton from one version of Latin London to a newer one. Recently, I returned to La Barra to find Maria-Luisa’s son Juan serving and the pica pollo as good as ever: five pieces of chicken with a thick jacket of batter that, in its death throes upon contact with hot oil, has twisted and spluttered into dark brown curlicues. At the weekend, you’ll find the restaurant packed to the rafters, the speakers blaring music from Cali as families share soups, bandeja paisa and excellent empanadas. Near them, inevitably, will be a table of young men tackling the biggest pica pollo available.

Name: Chez Bruce
Description:
Rank: 88

Food writers with a time machine only want one thing: to go back to Harveys in 1987 when Marco was sweating noradrenaline and taste the meal that launched a thousand imitators. Chez Bruce is the closest thing we have. It occupies the same space on Wandsworth Common and shares the same restaurateur in Nigel Platts-Martin, but there is something of the land that time forgot about it, with a menu reassuringly 20 years behind trends. Fay Maschler once said that Chez Bruce, for its unwavering consistency, is a more impressive restaurant than Harveys, and the dishes I want here are the ones that feel like you’re ingesting that technique-led lineage, particularly the impossibly-rich stuffed trotter (taken from Marco, who took it from Pierre Koffmann), which is usually only on the menu in February. A special shout to the cheese board, which is the dictionary definition of ‘well kept’, and the first one that has ever made me understand having cheese as a course.

Name: Zeret Kitchen
Description:
Rank: 87

In truth, almost any Ethiopian or Eritrean restaurant in South London would be at home on this list – we’re blessed with Rhoda, Ge’ez, Habesha, Saint Gabriel and countless more. But Zeret Kitchen on Camberwell Road is the one I keep gravitating to, partly because it’s one of the few that can attract both the art students and aunties wearing netelas, and partly because its owner Tafe Belayneh is a constant, reassuring presence, greeting you across the threshold as if you’ve entered her home. Belayneh works alchemy with lentils: her misir wot has an uncanny meaty depth of slow-cooked ragù, while the defin misir wot has the acidic butteriness of cottage cheese. The veg dishes are so strong that Zeret frequently gets mislabelled as a vegan restaurant, but the meat is equally good, particularly the spiced tartare of Belayneh’s special kitfo, or dulet – kidneys and tripe finely chopped into springy anonymity – which could win over even the most ardent offal sceptic.

Name: J. Sheekey
Description:
Rank: 86

In two decades, Richard Caring has managed to squander most of the precious inheritance he gained from the acquisition of Jeremy King and Chris Corbin’s restaurants: Le Caprice is shut, while The Ivy has become a chain more suited to mid-sized towns. And yet J. Sheekey remains happily unmarred, retaining the veneer of luxury that Corbin and King added to transform Sheekey’s into Theatreland’s own version of Musso & Frank’s. The standard menu – bar a pneumatic must-order cheddar soufflé – is entirely seafood and pudding: a fish pie, translucent skate in brown butter and capers, a grotesquely over-the-top lobster thermidor that comes with some of London’s best fries (not chips, despite what the menu says), an architecturally sound banoffee ice cream choux. The hunter green banquettes, the panelled walls filled with actors’ photos, the couple celebrating their golden wedding anniversary at the next table, the feeling of being anywhere except Leicester Square – all of this is restaurant-making as misdirection and stagecraft.

Name: B&K Salt Beef Bar
Description:
Rank: 85

One of the peculiarities – and joys – of living in London is how an institution like the Jewish salt beef bar can survive through the stewardship of a Cypriot family: the Georgious. While the Tongue & Briskets in central London are run by the third-generation Georgious, it’s still worth going up to the original B&K in Edgware, which was started by Bambos almost 50 years ago and is now run by his sons Michael and Jonny. This is a sandwich shop for purists: thick slices of tongue or salt beef and little else, washed down with chicken soup, with a sweet fish ball thrown in for dessert. But there is space for amendments. Personally, I like to ask Michael or Jonny for extra mustard, while food writer Daniel Young has a technique for getting the brothers to give him extra fat. The youngest Georgiou, Marina, once told me that at the Pinner branch, you can convince them to add fried egg and ketchup, although this is pushing it, even for me.

Name: Sweetings
Description: Rank: 84

Name: Sông Quê
Description: Rank: 83

Name: Imone
Description:
Rank: 82

When I get off the train at New Malden and feel the sense of calm that Hangeul on Surrey concrete brings me, I make a beeline for Imone: Junghwa Song’s small restaurant that means ‘Aunt’s place’ and promises homeliness. As London’s Korean restaurants become more refined, the saengseon jjim at Imone – a whole bisected whiting, sharp teeth jutting out, so haphazardly covered in a bundle of chrysanthemum greens that it’s difficult to know where they end and the fish begins – is a reassuringly ugly dish. The whole thing is covered in a chilli-heavy sauce that packs enough heat to compel you to switch back and forth between it, the firm, salty flesh of the whiting and the bitter-herbaceousness of the greens. In terms of great London Korean dishes, it’s up there with the galbijjim at Miga, the jajangmyeon at You Me, and Imone’s own crispy pajeon, which is still the best version of the dish you’re going to find west of Seoul and east of LA.

Name: Molesey Fish Bar
Description:
Rank: 81

It’s become a cliché to baldly state that ‘London has no good fish and chips’, so it’s doubly annoying to bear the sad news that the best chippy in London isn’t technically in London. Run by Cypriot brothers Chris and Steven Georgallou, Molesey Fish Bar near Hampton Court is one of the last ‘London’ chippies to still fry in beef dripping. The aroma will hit you before you see the shop: sharp, barnyard, overripe, like tropical fruit left out in a bowl out in the sun. If it’s your first visit, then I suggest getting fish and some of the best chips you will ever have – sweet from the dripping and soft inside, as if the potato has sublimated from the heat. Only then can you move onto the Georgallous’ most lethal invention, the Stav: doner meat (get the chicken) and chips in pitta, their warmth melting two slices of American cheese. It is the most consequential gastronomic event to take place in Hampton Court since Henry VIII contracted gout.

Name: The Ledbury
Description:
Rank: 80

I hope it’s not damning with faint praise to say that The Ledbury is the most interesting Michelin three-starred restaurant operating in London right now. It is an anomaly among the six, which are either of the Gordon-Ramsay or hotel-restaurant school and have a tendency to feel rootless. Instead, The Ledbury is the high-watermark of a whole tide of London restaurants, which runs from Chez Bruce and the Phil Howard era of The Square through to 40 Maltby Street and The Clove Club, which are headed by Ledbury alums. This lineage is filled with elegant French-ish food, but The Ledbury also zooms in on British produce (particularly muscular game, venison and pork) and incorporates outside influences (amazake, makrut lime, an array of fragrant tisanes) in a way that feels less studied than its rivals – a consequence of chef Brett Graham’s Antipodean restlessness. I only wish I had eaten here before it received Michelin’s top honour: there is a simpler restaurant to be found here, underneath all the stars.

Name: Bocca di Lupo
Description: Rank: 79

Name: Bentley’s
Description:
Rank: 78

You don’t go to Bentley’s to be seduced – you can go to J. Sheekey or Scott’s for that. You go to Bentley’s if you are one of those strange people interested in every animal that comes out of the sea and are willing to pay well for the absolute best of them. Bentley’s is my favourite place in London to eat oysters from around Great Britain and Ireland, but also all manner of cold seafood. Cold whelks, the pauper’s oyster, are a fetish only seafood lovers have, and here they are given the respect they deserve: served ice cold in their prehistoric shells, dense, with a firm snap. Specials are often where it’s at: where else, besides a Japanese izakaya, would you find herring milt, deep-fried and devilled, in garlic butter, as good as any sweetbread? Personally, I go to Bentley’s to remember that, although many things have changed, London is still a port city.

Name: Saikei
Address: Holiday Inn Express, 85 Bugsby’s Way, SE10 0GD
Description:
Rank: 77

Say what you like about Saikei – that it’s hard to get to, that it’s located in a Holiday Inn Express, that it’s spiritually a Los Angeles restaurant transported to the Docklands but only offers discount parking – but is there any London restaurant that gives so many people so much joy week in, week out? There is truly nothing like it on a Sunday, when the 200-strong room ripples with the feeling of a huge party that you’ve somehow just crashed. Ever since I was inducted into dim sum as a child at New World (RIP), this has always been the atmosphere I’ve yearned for: East End Cantonese accents, families of 12 eating salt and pepper lobster, checkboxing my order like a multiple-choice exam, a kinesis of waiters ferrying dumplings. Everything is about two notches better than it needs to be, and the spicy chicken and green pepper ho fun (a dish my editor Adam Coghlan introduced me to) is exceptional.

Name: Cafe Cecilia
Description:
Rank: 76

There are two very Londonish tendencies in the food at Max Rocha’s Cafe Cecilia – a restaurant where filigree fritti sit alongside mince on beef dripping toast. The first is the bright Mediterranean cuisine that runs through The River Cafe (Rocha’s alma mater), which is capable of bringing sunshine into a room that overlooks a decommissioned Hackney gas ring. The second is the earthiness of solid, St. John country cooking, in this case drawn from Rocha’s Irish background. These tendencies are sometimes at odds with each other and sometimes capable of producing something generative, but the best cooking here often has the no-nonsense simplicity of booting a clearance into row Z – like an onglet steak with the charred sear of a Whopper, or that mince on toast, which is nothing less than the purest expression of Worcestershire sauce. Unadornment is a virtue here, which is why Cecilia is the only one of the new-wave cafes that understands breakfast.

Name: Roketsu
Address: 12 New Quebec Street, W1H 7RW Note: since this was written, Roketsu has changed menus and chefs, and we can no longer recommend it without a revisit.
Description: Rank: 75

Name: Antepliler/Antepliler Doner/Antepliler Ciger & Beyran/Antepliler Kunefe
Address: Restaurant: 45–46 Green Lanes, Harringay Ladder, N4 1AG Doner: 43 Grand Parade, Green Lanes, Harringay Ladder, N4 1AQ Ciger & Beyran: 44 Grand Parade, Green Lanes, Harringay Ladder, N4 1AG Kunefe: 441 Green Lanes, Haringey N4 1HA
Description:
Rank: 74

Picking a Green Lanes ocakbaşi is like supporting a football team: you get to choose once and then you’re stuck with it for life. Antepliler is an exception, because it offers something the others don’t. When its founder Ahmet Üstünsürmeli opened it in the early nineties, it was as a baklava shop; since then, he has added shopfront after shopfront of specialised businesses, from the main restaurant and takeaway lahmacun to, in quick succession, an offal specialist (now reopened after a decade hiatus), kunefe shop and doner restaurant. The result is that, across five businesses, you can pick and choose some of the best dishes on the street: İskender, cut thin from two vast and trunkless legs of lamb and covered at the table with hot melted butter; thin skewers of liver and sweetbread, served St. John-style with a punchy parsley and onion salad; and its unimpeachable lahmacun, as close to a true North London pizza style as we’ll ever get.

Name: Saffron Kitchen
Description: Rank: 73

Name: Nissi
Description:
Rank: 72

Like dim sum restaurants, Cypriot tavernas in North London seem to exist on a spectrum: at one end are places that prioritise good food, and at the other are those that deliver great vibes in rooms covered in New River bougainvillea. Andy Panayiotou and Carlos Charalambous’s Nissi is slightly too prim for a proper, vibey Palmers Green taverna, but the food is even better than anything I remember from my childhood. At some tavernas you fill up on too many bought-in dips that bloat you before the fish arrives; at Nissi everything is timed to the second, from the dips and vegetables (fasolakia that actually tastes of the bean; salty, intense tarama) to the hot starters (a globe of kolokithokeftede that collapses like a soufflé; unimprovable fresh calamari). The fish course in particular is a barnstormer – a small gang of crispy red mullets, and a skewer of swordfish so burnished by the grill that the char forms a second skin. On food alone, this is the best taverna in the city.

Name: Sollip
Description:
Rank: 71

There is a version of Woongchul Park and Bomee Ki’s Korean-ish restaurant that I would want to eat at every week, which is a strange thing to say about a restaurant as intricate and corseted as Sollip. It would involve a large portion of Park’s sot-bap (which arrives seething in a cast iron pan, with a layer of crispy rice ready to be scraped out with a paddle), and a side of something barbecued – perhaps a pork jowl glazed in doenjang, with a layer of fat as thin as the gel in an After Eight. Then there would be a course of Korean teas with Ki’s magical desserts, ending with an oozing black sesame madeleine or a Wicked-Witch-of-the-West-green mugwort madeleine. However, this is London, so this lunchroom–teahouse hybrid doesn’t exist. Instead, Sollip has to be content with its Michelin star and operating one of London’s most elegant tasting menus, while I have to be content with Sollip being a once-a-year treat.

Name: Phở Thuý Tây Café
Description:
Rank: 70

Thúy Nguyễn may not serve your favourite phở in London, but she serves mine: a quiet, unassuming northern-style phở with a crystalline broth that I could drink for breakfast. Since Nguyễn first opened Phở Thuý Tây in Deptford in 2013, she has been a flagbearer for dishes popular with young Vietnamese students in Hanoi and now in London – steaming goat hot pots with plastic bags of rau răm, or intestines dipped in mắm tôm, a bureaucratic grey paste that tastes like the funk of a thousand prawn heads reduced to the density of a neutron star. Now the restaurant has moved again, from Old Kent Road to Surrey Quays, I have gravitated away from offal and towards Nguyen’s simpler cooking, like the crispy noodles bound together into round, rösti-like pucks, the cinnabar-warmth of the thit kho, or her unadorned phở. And as more Vietnamese students come to the UK looking for home comforts, Phở Thuý Tây increasingly looks like the future.

Name: Vasantha Vilas
Description:
Rank: 69

If you’re stuck for choice on what to order at this East Ham Tamil canteen, whose menu runs longer than some religious texts, then Vasantha Vilas offers a salve for the indecisive. The first is the mini tiffin, which gives you a dosa whose edges taste like a toasted cheese crisp, a lightly-spiced vada, two idli, a selection of chutneys, and (my favourite) pongal, which has the stiff consistency of a cream-heavy rice pudding. The second (if you ignore the Indo-Chinese and north Indian stuff) is the south Indian thali, which gives you six faultless vegetable curries (usually okra, spinach, beans and something else), whose complexity is only undermined by the likelihood that your favourite single bite will be the taste of plain white rice covered in a teaspoon of sweet ghee. Owners Kannan Murugan and Mohamed Thasleem have recently expanded the restaurant into Surbiton and Orpington, which means that Vasantha Vilas may soon be our own homegrown Saravanaa Bhavan.

Name: Namak Mandi
Description:
Rank: 68

Like many Londoners, my first introduction to Pashtun cooking was at Hamid Jan’s three-storied Namak Mandi in Tooting, where karahis start their life in front of you as a bobbing mass of tomatoes and meat. Come to Namak Mandi late on in the evening and the restaurant will be in a bustling state of well-managed disarray – groups of young men in the carpeted window seats sharing hot, sweet tea; families arguing over who got there first; waiters climbing the stairs to the private rooms – but you can have a more relaxed time at the new branch opposite. A recent visit confirmed that the chapli kebabs, sent out like funeral boats in a sea of bubbling animal fat and arriving at the table with a solid half-centimetre of blackened crust, are still first among equals. However, the essential dish here is the gola karahi: seekh kebabs that add a note of smoke to a flawless layered gravy, the hidden third option between the karahi and the grill.

Name: Calong
Description:
Rank: 67

Calong synthesises two recent (and welcome) London trends: the desire of chefs who’ve toiled anonymously at institutions to come out from the dark and cook what they really want to cook, and the sudden surge of interest in Korean food. Joo Young Won used to be the head chef at Galvin at Windows but has swapped Mayfair for Stoke Newington Church Street, where he investigates the shared architecture of Korean and French cuisine. Calong dares to ask questions like: what if you served jjamppong as a bouillabaisse, with a scoop of aioli, or tried to infuse an onglet steak with all the intensity of a bulgogi? Sometimes when chefs do this, the result veers ruinously towards over-intellectualising, but there is real soul in what Won is doing here. Desserts by Won’s partner Sujin are a particular strength, each one delivering more than promised, while the cramped room has the pent-up energy of the old Singburi.

Name: Plates
Description: Rank: 66

Name: Graam Bangla
Description:
Rank: 65

When Graam Bangla reopened in 2019 under chef Atikur Rahman and owner Shanur Ali, the aim was to transform it from a male-dominated canteen to a welcoming space to learn about Sylheti and wider Bangladeshi cuisine. Luckily, the food itself was untampered with. Let waiters guide you through the glass display of river fishes – some in curries, some small enough to eat whole, some reworked (I have a fondness for the fish ball curry, each one the size of a golf ball). Vegetables seem innocuous but are where you should watch out: the green beans with bichi have the fermented punch of shrimp paste and the olfactory haze of a can of kerosene. Start with bhorthas rolled into balls and presented on a plate like a selection of bath bombs, before you paint your canvas of white rice with as many different curries as you can. The only thing I order every time is the tarka dal – with barely more texture than broth, it provides a respite from everything else.

Name: Trivet
Description:
Rank: 64

There are two ways of eating at Trivet, Jonny Lake and Isa Bal’s two-Michelin-starred restaurant tucked in a shard-shaped room round the back of London Bridge. The first is as one of the few fine-dining restaurants without a tasting menu, where you can order L’Arpège-priced mains. The second – and more interesting – way is to treat it as a neighbourhood wine bar that happens to serve experimental food. You could come here and order a Domaine Tempier rosé with an ox tongue roll that comes with blackcurrants so sweet and tart that it’s ontologically pudding, or a deconstructed Turkish breakfast that reworks simit into a sesame-encrusted cake with yoghurt ice cream and black olive caramel, one of the few modernist dishes in the city that feels like it belongs to London. The butter pies – a great Canadian contribution to food culture and a relic of Lake’s upbringing – are exceptional, with a filling so molten you could easily use them to gel your hair.

Name: Noble Rot Mayfair
Description:
Rank: 63

I admire Noble Rot’s ability to adapt to a new market. Dan Keeling and Mark Andrew’s third restaurant, in Mayfair’s Shepherd Market, winks at members’ club 5 Hertford Street across the road, and so chef Adam Wood has engineered a menu for the enclave that reads conservative but tastes delicious. This is mostly achieved via a series of subtle twists: mustard rabbit is served with a Pog-sized pool of pickled walnut sauce, a detail more Henderson than Escoffier; cod cheeks come with a bronzed comet tail of batter and a ‘curry’ dipping sauce of what is essentially chicken makhani gravy. Apple crumble, so often a tripwire for chefs too keen to innovate, is played almost completely straight, with correctly uneven clusters of crumble. The only concession is a bright stem ginger ice cream, a detail which, like the others, feels correct rather than clever. It is currently the best Noble Rot restaurant – a testament to the group’s ability to shape shift without losing their essence.

Name: Al Kahf
Description:
Rank: 62

I remember when Al Kahf was essentially a prayer room with a restaurant attached; to get there, you had to go through one of those Dickensian Whitechapel alleys you thought didn’t exist anymore, down some stairs and into what appeared to be a social club. There was no menu, except the one in your waiter’s head. I loved that restaurant, but it has been a pleasure to watch Al Kahf grow into what it is today. On my last visit, the owner Mohammed Jama, rocked by another viral TikTok, was busy greeting Muslim customers who had come from as far as Australia just to get Al Kahf’s bariis iskukaris, served with lamb shoulder or shank. The lamb falls off the bone like a shrug, in layers of sweet fat and crispy skin, and is served alongside spiced rice sweetened with currants and enriched with the lamb’s own broth. The only accompaniment needed is a squeezy bottle of basbaas.

Name: The Cocochine
Description:
Rank: 61

In a city untethered from the land, The Cocochine’s terroir is money – a Mayfair townhouse restaurant supplied almost entirely by a Northamptonshire farm and a private Scottish island owned by one of its investors. Yet I sometimes wish more rich people would open follies like this. It allows chef Larry Jayasekara cheap access to some of the best British produce bar none, which then finds its way onto a £39 three-course menu – probably the best-value fine-dining lunch in the city. You might get a raviolo of bracingly fresh langoustine in a spiced, coconut broth (Jayasekara’s Sri Lankan background is used sincerely, never just as an accent to put on), a bruiser of a beef pie, a sweet flan that is secretly watalappam, or jaggery caramel on ice cream flecked with so much vanilla that it’s almost boozy. Fine-dining majordomo Andy Hayler feels that the (bizarrely Michelin-starless) Cocochine is using better ingredients than any three-star restaurant in London. He is right.

Name: Taste of Pakistan
Description:
Rank: 60

Some of the initial thrill of Taste of Pakistan is simply down to getting a booking. It may be in the middle of nowhere on a Hounslow arterial road, but it has become one of the most perpetually full restaurants in London, helped by its adrenaline-racing take on Pakistani Pashtun cooking and its charismatic owner, Naseer Khan, who has the air of someone who could either be a wrestler or an imam. Even as Pashtun cuisine has become more common, the food at Taste of Pakistan is worth travelling for: chapli kebabs, thick as hubcaps, pockmarked with coriander seeds; acidic charsi karahis; outstanding grill cooking and naans the size of torsos. Because Nas chooses violence in his replies to people’s negative Google reviews, there is an element of fear surrounding Taste of Pakistan, which results in a rowdy atmosphere of people delighted just to be inside – a Berghain for people who love lamb.

Name: Sushi Tetsu
Description:
Rank: 59

I have attended wedding receptions that run shorter than the time it takes to finish a meal at Sushi Tetsu, a seven-seater sushi bar in Clerkenwell run with an almost-religious secrecy by husband and wife Toru and Harumi Takahashi. But it rewards patience. There isn’t a better straight sushi meal in London: bite after bite of pristine, faultless nigiri dissolve like PaperMints, ending with an astonishing layered tamago, Toru’s signature. So much of your experience here will rely on how well you get on with your fellow diners once you run out of things to talk about with Toru (who, as befits a sushi master, once played the part of Flea in a Red Hot Chili Peppers cover band). If going to Endo at the Rotunda is like watching a one-man play, Tetsu is shared improv over four hours. It may be a consequence of its no-photos policy, but even now I remember the experience of sitting through the meal more than I remember the remarkable food.

Name: Casse-Croûte
Description:
Rank: 58

In a city obsessed with newness, it’s easy to forget that Casse-Croûte has been there on a corner of Bermondsey Street for 12 years just doing its stuff – that is, serving some of the best French bistro cooking in London about 30 years after (and nine years before) it became de rigeur to do so. The form of Hervé Durochat and Sylvain Soulard’s menu is still the same as when it opened: three starters, three or four mains and three desserts, ever changing and written entirely on a blackboard in unreadably cursive French. It’s difficult to give precise recommendations for a menu that is this protean, but I have never regretted the decision to order a pithivier or anything described as ‘en croûte’ or ‘à partager’; proper-noun sauces, plutocratic in their richness, are also a real strength. Because these are adult plates of food, dessert can often be a step too far, but I know people who have a Google Alert set for Casse-Croûte’s millefeuille.

Name: Ognisko
Description:
Rank: 57

When people ask me to recommend a restaurant for an age-diverse group, one that includes people who want good food and drink but also those who crave the feeling of luxury and comfortable seats, I inevitably turn to Ognisko, located in the Polish Hearth Club in South Kensington. It has an excellent bar, where, with a strong horseradish vodka martini in one hand, you have a vista to the handsome dining room, at once opulent and intimate. Jan Woroniecki, who has overseen Ognisko’s resurgence from old-stager to culinary destination, has made sure that the food here is far better than the room needs it to be: potato pancakes served with blushing pink chicken livers; a huge schnitzel à la Holstein that beats the one at the Wolseley; a multi-layered honey cake, like a millefeuille of Graham crackers. Make sure, whatever you do, to get two carafes of vodka on ice – one for the food, and one for the road.

Name: Miga
Description:
Rank: 56

The family behind Miga – the Kos – can claim to have influenced three different phases of Korean cooking in the city: from the father Hyun Sang’s first restaurant in New Malden, to the mother Kyung Suk Lee’s takeaway in Morden, to Miga v3 in London Fields, where the sons Jae Hun and Jae Kyum, dressed head to toe in black Issey Pleats, act as hypemen for their dad’s cooking: the classics executed with unusual flair. Taste Hyun Sang’s fresh and galvanising kimchi, or his seolleongtang, milky with collagen and sipped at the end of the meal with as much ceremony as a bowl of matcha, and you’ll realise how long London has been crying out for restaurant-ified Korean home cooking like this. The galbijjim is as good as any I’ve had, including at strip malls in Los Angeles, with each element – rib, potato, carrot – soaking up the short-rib broth, as intense and concentrated as a beef eau de vie.

Name: Haringey Corbacisi
Address: Unit 7 Salisbury Road, Green Lanes, N8 0RX
Description:
Rank: 55

As an ocakbaşi arms race continues to consume Green Lanes, we need to value specialists like Haringey Corbacisi. Before its recent glow-up, the restaurant sold only variations of soup and sulu yemek, the kind of simple stews made from beans, aubergine or lamb neck that you would be content to eat with a plate of bulgur every day for the rest of your life. Although it now has a grill section, nothing I have tried so far has persuaded me to veer away from the soups, particularly the kelle paça. Behind the counter you might spot a pyramid of lamb skulls stacked on top of one another like a warlord’s threat; these are stripped of all their meat, separated out into head, tongue, brains and eyes and added to the long-simmered broth as per the customer’s request. Each time I eat this dish, with a few pickles and olives, often late at night after a game of snooker upstairs, I wonder why I bother eating anything else.

Name: Lahori Nihaari
Description:
Rank: 54

There are two truly famous London dals. One is the unctuous black dal at Dishoom, now endlessly copied and reiterated. The other is the dal maash at Upton Park’s Lahori Nihaari – an angry traffic-light green, yellow and red of coriander, lentil and ghee, as fierce and pungent as Dishoom’s is mild and creamy. It’s what your Punjabi grandad might, in a fit of passion, call a ‘proper dal’. In theory, you could just come for that and the burnished sesame kulcha – a paragon of restaurant breadmaking – and have a great vegetarian lunch, but you’d be missing out on many other things. The paiye soup, for instance, which comes with a small lamb trotter – the cornerstone of any beauty regime – which uncles in kufis will skilfully strip down to tiny bones, or the karahis, reduced to their sticky essence, which arrive in metal pans of escalating sizes (from large to larger) with on-bone meat and quantities of ginger normally reserved for antiseptic treatments.

Name: Takahashi
Description:
Rank: 53

A dinner at Takahashi, a 12-seater Japanese restaurant in Wimbledon, unfolds in two halves. It starts with six or seven courses of snacks prepared behind a curtain by Nobuhisa Takahashi and served by his wife Yuko – perhaps a delicate mini-Arctic roll of prawn and crab tempura encasing the fresh snap of a green bean, or a perfectly set shot of porcini and kombu chawanmushi with a layer of melted parmesan, a dish that is to umami what the espresso is to bitterness. For the second half, Taka comes out and makes sushi: nothing avant garde, just nine pieces of austerely dressed fish – wild salmon from the Faroes, the butterfat of a torched Hokkaido scallop, a maki roll with tuna so finely chopped it has the mouthfeel of an emulsion. One of Takahashi’s aims is to provide a nutritionally balanced menu rather than hit after hit – and, somehow, after three hours of this stuff, you feel lighter than when you came in.

Name: Quo Vadis
Description:
Rank: 52

Some buildings have souls – all we can hope to be is the temporary custodians of them. 26–28 Dean Street, for example, has been a brothel, Karl Marx’s flat, and several doomed restaurants all with the name Quo Vadis. That is until 2011 when, like a slot machine landing on three bells, it received its perfect chef in Jeremy Lee, its perfect proprietors in the Hart Brothers, and its perfect designer in John Broadley. Just over a decade on, it feels like it’s been this way for a century. The food is what it always should have been: a mix of old Soho glamour and modern British rakishness, crowdpleasers (including kickshaws and pies) that wear their lineages lightly and a truly brilliant eel sandwich that is a study in minimalism. However, Lee’s puddings, billowy and excessive, are pure maximalism: I once ate a dessert here in which I counted four different variations of cream.

Name: Royal China Club
Description:
Rank: 51

Is Royal China Club the best dimsum restaurant in London? Saikei and Yi-Ban will give you the Sunday service vibe, if that’s what you crave, while Dimsum & Duck, whose chef Henry Chow used to be executive chef at Royal China Club, will deliver similar quality but with the distractions of a massive queue. It’s still worth shelling out for the original. The dumplings are still coiled mini-masterpieces of textural contrast: har gau as delicate as wagashi; red rice rolls with wrappers of Atsuko Kudo latex, grainy with sesame and filled with crispy prawn; char siu pork puffs that may well be shortened with lard but taste like butter, flaking off like a rich French pastry. Royal China Club is also the one of the few places in London that serves proper double-boiled medicinal soups: a teal and 30-year-old tangerine peel number will set you back over £30 for a few gulps, but has a bitter intensity that could raise the dead.

Name: Chishuru
Description:
Rank: 50

When it comes to West African fine dining, you are either an Akoko person or a Chishuru person – just like you might be a Sinner or Alcaraz person. One is ruthlessly perfect; the other is flawed, human, but with the capacity, every so often, to force you out of your chair. I admire both, but I am a Chishuru person because I love food in which you can feel the presence of the chef. Joké Bakare’s cuisine takes in not just Lagos, but the north of Nigeria and the rest of West Africa – a pan-Africanism that is part of Bakare’s heritage and politics. Since Chishuru moved from Brixton to Fitzrovia and gained a Michelin star two years ago it has become less casual, but the dishes are still recognisably Bakare’s, showcasing the region’s unique spices: goat ayamase with the dark-chocolate musk of iru, an ingot of ekuru with the consistency of a cumulonimbus, and a party jollof, which comes for the table and can be refreshed if you ask.

Name: Brawn
Description:
Rank: 49

How often, when faced with the crippling indecision of choosing between the latest on-trend openings, has Shoreditch heard the line, ‘But we could just go to Brawn?’ On those murky, lightless London evenings, it appears on Columbia Road like a mirage of hospitality – warm ambience, a glass of wine served at the right temperature and a menu of things you actually want to eat. Since Ed Wilson opened Brawn in 2010 at the start of the East London wine-bar movement, it has settled into its location like a pair of raw denim jeans. A recent wintery menu had nothing more ambitious on it than some pasta and braises – but what pasta and what braises! – all confidently seasoned. Even a portion of nervetti – beef tendons cooked to wine-gum chewiness – is an excuse for serving a correctly cooked and acidulated plate of beans. This comfort in its own skin is the reason why Brawn continues to survive when everything around it has been and gone.

Name: The French House
Description: Rank: 48

Name: D&K Gambian
Description: Rank: 47

Name: Peckham Bazaar
Description:
Rank: 46

The outstanding ‘Greek’ restaurant in London, like some of the best Greek restaurants in Thessaloniki, is run by an Albanian – in this case John Gionleka, who operates the sometimes-forgotten Peckham Bazaar on a residential sidestreet in SE15. A proud, red-blooded Greek chef having to self-censor along national lines couldn’t have opened Peckham Bazaar, but Gionleka is at liberty to pick and choose dishes from across the Balkans, Greece, Cyprus and Turkey, fusing them into a supra-cuisine that veers from adjika (adorning the lamb kebabs) to Izmir meatballs – or, rather, he knows that it’s all the same cuisine anyway. Seafood cooking is a notable strength, with extraordinary calamari that tastes of holidays and an emphasis on bringing the best out of small-to-medium fish like mullets and dories, faithfully translating a Balkan approach to British ingredients. What is most impressive is the kitchen’s lack of fear when it comes to undercomplication, stripping away every extraneous ingredient. What’s left is called ‘style’.

Name: Café Deco
Description:
Rank: 45

I first sat up straight and took notice of Anna Tobias when she put a dish of carrot râpées on the menu at P. Franco in 2018. It seemed to run counter to the prevailing logic of London menus, where there must always be a competitive hero dish to grab the attention of fickle, Instagram-scrolling diners. You don’t travel for carrot râpées. At Deco, since 2020, Tobias has continued where she left off, constructing menus that follow her own internal logic. There will be soups and stews that could appear at the table of a Balkan grandmother, an egg mayo that is literally two lobes of egg set in a blanket of yellow taffeta, suet puddings in a pool of warm custard. There is always the question about charging restaurant prices for dinnerlady food, but when it’s done with such sincerity it never comes off as provocation. It feels, quite simply, like food you want to eat.

Name: Wolkite
Description:
Rank: 44

The bar for Ethiopian and Eritrean food in London is now so high that it’s difficult to spot which restaurant might be leading the pack. But Wolkite, run by Mekdes Siware in the shadow of the Emirates Stadium, is my pick, by a hair. Order a mix of vegetarian dishes and you might notice the flair that has gone into each one: the aggressiveness and diversity of the spicing, the ability to make each lentil dish taste distinct rather than like variations on a theme, the strong backbone of gram flour in the shiro wot that ties it all together. The kitfo, which Wolkite used to be named after, is outstanding, but I truly love the lamb ribs (which are second only to those at Umut 2000) and the asa wot, a fish stew that you will be hard-pressed to find anywhere else. A final word for the tej, Wolkite’s homemade honey wine, which is genuinely better than most London craft meads.

Name: Uncle Wrinkle
Description: Rank: 43

Name: Durak Tantuni
Description:
Rank: 42

When people talk forlornly about the paucity of London’s late night culture, I always take them to mean that they wish there were more places like Durak Tantuni, a tantuni specialist on West Green Road where it only starts to get busy around midnight and continues to heat up into the early hours. There is nothing on the menu here except tantuni – Turkey’s strong counter to the taco – and there are only two decisions you need to make. The first is whether to get it as lavaş or bread. Owner Dogan Yesil, or one of his assistants, then fries the meat to order in a pan resembling an upside-down sombrero, judiciously adds onions, sumac and parsley, and then, with the sprezzatura of the coolest person you know rolling a cigarette, applies a slick of meat fat to seal the whole package. An inedible amount of pickles and lemon are provided gratis. Then, all you need to do is decide whether to get another.

Name: Cafe TPT
Description:
Rank: 41

On nine out of ten Chinatown days, you will find me at Wong Kei, spending ten minutes and seven pounds on a soup. But when I’m feeling rich or depressed, I will inevitably end up at Cafe TPT, a restaurant that can do the whole Wong Kei menu backwards and in high heels, for a little bit extra. TPT is a template for how all Cantonese restaurants in London can and should be – competent at everything and exceptional at a select few standouts. There’s the creamy beef flank curry that reduces down in its stone pot, or the blistered, caramelised green beans, or the pork chop Macau-style with onions and cheesy béchamel – a chaise longue of a comfort dish, best eaten in the late hours to soak up a Soho night. I cannot be objective about this place. The most meaningful relationship of my adult life is the one I have with the laoban, who, in 15 years, has acknowledged that I’m a regular on exactly two occasions.

Name: Levant Book Café
Description: Rank: 40

Name: Camille
Description:
Rank: 39

When it opened, Camille was unfairly lumped into the ‘French brasserie named after a woman’ moment of 2023. In reality, Camille is the most successful of the St. John bastards, a group of modern London restaurants which have pushed the idea of ‘nose to tail’ to its seams and whose argot is as at ease with supermarket condiments as with regenerative agriculture and whole-animal butchery. Chef Elliot Hashtroudi has a love of monumental flavours: smoked fish and crustacean heads become condiments for meat, while offal is sometimes used as a provocation (if you order snout, you will get something that looks like a child’s drawing of a snout). However, there’s real technique anchoring it all – a dish of calves brains with purslane, for instance, could honour any trad bouchon. There’s something admirably freewheeling about Camille, a sense that it is making things up on the spot; it’s this spirit that stops its disparate elements from remaining clichés, instead becoming something wholly original.

Name: The Devonshire
Description: Rank: 38

Name: Tasty Jerk
Description:
Rank: 37

When the wind catches the smoke right, you don’t need to worry about directions as you walk up Whitehorse Lane in Thornton Heath – the scent of barbecued meat from Tasty Jerk’s chimney extraction will hit you from a mile away. There was a time, when its founder Murphy Lawrence still worked there, that I would have told you that eating the Tasty Jerk jerk pork was one of the top three things you’re legally allowed to do in public in London. Although it doesn’t always hit those supreme heights under new management, nowhere else has taken its crown. The jerk pork doesn’t need sauce: bite into it dry and you can taste the long, careful cooking of the meat, the sting of Scotch bonnets, the breakdown of connective tissue, the fat rendering and crisping – soft as chicharrón and sweeter than the best siu yuk – decades’ worth of seasoning from the three blackened drums, and notes of char, soot and petroleum that rush up your nose and down your throat. The chicken is good too.

Name: Mountain
Description:
Rank: 36

What do you do when your first restaurant becomes the most-liked place in the city? Open somewhere as baffling as Mountain, of course. Tomos Parry’s difficult second restaurant is less people-pleasing than Brat, but it’s the one that keeps compelling me to return, its vast menu begging the question of what the best version of Mountain actually is. It’s not the grill, which you can go to Brat for. It could be the dishes that display recherché technique, like the Maillard-less patina of a spider crab omelette, whose money shot once provoked a table next to me to dissolve into raptures of delight. But I think Mountain is best experienced through small assemblages of cutting-edge produce that show off its sourcing, such as cured dairy beef with enough lactic funk to be its own self-contained cheeseburger, and through its braises, particularly a garnet-coloured tripe dish filled with so much collagen it sticks your lips together. I wouldn’t mind if restaurant three just did stews.

Name: Towpath
Description:
Rank: 35

The sighting of Towpath open after its four-month hibernation is the East-London-white-person equivalent of spotting the Eid moon – a sign of renewal. Lori de Mori and chef Laura Jackson’s canal-side cafe has consequently become synonymous with a style of light, vernal cooking: small plates of green things, undressed asparagus spears with a dip, fizzing, bright salads. And yet, I would like to make a case that Jackson’s best cooking is her sometimes entirely unseasonal larger dishes that seem to have wandered in from another restaurant entirely: a golden matzo ball soup of unimpeachable clarity, chicken meatballs with beans and parmesan that makes a case for the supremacy of spherical chicken, brisket with tzimmes that could put Reich’s out of business. I sometimes wonder what Jackson is doing for the other third of the year – there’s a great Ashkenazi Jewish deli hiding here, and the fact that there’s nowhere cosy to have her winter cooking is a minor London tragedy.

Name: Sikatiô
Description:
Rank: 34

A diasporic Ivorian restaurant as accomplished as Sikatiô should, by rights, be in Paris. And yet, improbably, it’s here in Brockley, where Lynda Beble and Brice Assemian are putting out some of the most skilful fish cooking in South London, including croaker in a deep-fried chainmail of skin – a show-stopping piece of soul food that tastes like if Colonel Sanders moved to the coast from deep Kentucky – and the soupe du pêcheur, a Satanic bouillabaisse of gently poached fish, crab and prawn with a broth that winds you with each gulp. There’s a strong sense of coup de grâce here, which extends to the meat dishes – lamb and guinea fowl suffused with wood smoke, or brisket in sauce graine, a gothic peanut soup made from the palm nut. My favourite thing on the entire menu might just be the fried plantain: cut on the diagonal and perfectly ripe, each piece has the same shape and sweetness as a teardrop.

Name: Leo’s
Description:
Rank: 33

Bright, the much-missed London Fields restaurant headed up by chefs Will Gleave and Giuseppe Belvedere, could never have lasted: it was like Simon and Garfunkel if there were two Paul Simons. While Gleave is now at Margate’s Sargasso, Belvedere has continued where he left off, at Clapton’s Leo’s, where he is putting out his most assured cooking to date. Eating here, in a city of mediocre pasta restaurants, can be a reminder of exactly what it is about Italian food that we’ve all fallen in love with: its generosity, directness and cheat-code flavour combinations. Riso al salto, the Milanese version of tahdig, is a simple dish – it’s just crispy, saffron rice – but adding a layer of fonduta transforms it into a decadent, savoury kind of truffle. Sharing mains, like a lasagne of gamey white ragù served with the spoon still in, or pork with a molten layer of Coombeshead ham, make it feel like you’re being cooked for by a friend who is secretly trying to seduce you.

Name: Em Sherif
Description:
Rank: 32

Lebanese cooking in London has settled – some might say ossified – into the grill and shawarma. Em Sherif counters this notion with its focus on what is really at the core of Lebanese cuisine: its salads and meze, its freshness and its opulent use of scented waters, spices and nuts. I don’t think any other restaurant in London has a bigger pine nut budget. There is a care devoted to small details that you normally don’t find outside the home in the explosive acidity of the fattoush, the baby-cheek delicacy of the dough in the lahme bi ajeen, and the hummus, as smooth and white as lime plaster. Yes, Em Sherif is an international chain. Yes, it is located in Harrods. Yes, the hummus starts at £16. But just have one bite of its grilled boneless poussin – an unintentional homage to the half-chicken on spicy rice at Lebo Grill – and you will agree that, if this is the price we have to pay, then so be it.

Name: Tawa Roti
Description:
Rank: 31

Anyone can make a curry, but making roti is a vocation. At Tawa Roti, a Trinidiadian takeaway in Clapham with a constant, self-refreshing stream of customers, that vocation is generational. It was opened in 2023 by Vash Mathura, the original owner of the legendary Roti Joupa, and passed on to his nephew Sean Mahabir, who continues the site’s legacy of introducing Londoners to good roti. The dhal puri roti skins here have no equal in the city. The thickness of two playing cards and slightly blistered from the tawa on the outside, they’re pliant enough that they hold the spiced split pea mixture and don’t rip from the weight of the filling. Get them with a mix of chana, pumpkin and spinach, add a macaroni pie – tangy with tamarind and with a jolt of black pepper – plus a portion of doubles, and you’ll have one of the best vegetarian meals money can buy. As Sean will warn you, just be careful with the pepper sauce.

Name: Asafo
Description:
Rank: 30

The kelewele at Asafo is plantain that has revealed its final form – a savoury, spicy fruit caramel-cooked almost to burning point. Covered in a shower of peanuts, it is the non-negotiable order at this Brixton Hill Ghanaian institution, the dish that every meal needs to start with before you move on to soups and stews, like tuo zaafi, a ball of swallow in a green–red yin-yang of okro and tomato. The atmosphere at Asafo on a busy evening – low lights, incongruous wallpaper, tall bottles of palm wine at every table – is akin to that of a backstage bar at a music venue. This is why one of my favourite things to do here is to treat it as a pub and order a beer and a portion of chofi, diabolical nuggets of turkey tails composed mostly of cholesterol to be dipped in shito. There’s a shambolic nature to Asafo that I love: on some days you may wait longer for mains than for the Second Coming, so make sure you’re having too good a time to care.

Name: Scotti’s Snack Bar
Description:
Rank: 29

Scotti’s on Clerkenwell Green is a more unusual establishment than it’s given credit for. Not quite a cafe, not quite a restaurant, this sandwich bar has no menu except the one that exists in the head of brothers Max and Al. Its clientele over the years has included light industry workers, cab drivers, and the gang who planned the Hatton Garden robbery. Today you’re more likely to find hip young Londoners looking for an escalope sandwich. Max understands that if it is made with dark meat and fried fresh to order, all an escalope sandwich needs is lemon juice, some raw onion and ‘Slim Shady’ (or ‘M&M’ – Al’s dad joke for mustard and mayo). It is the only escalope sandwich I know of that I would describe as ‘elegant’ – old London and new London all at once. Get it with a cappelletti in brodo imported from the shuttered restaurant next door, La Rocchetta (whose last Facebook update simply states, ‘if we don’t know you, you are not coming in for a sing song’).

Name: The Yellow Bittern
Description:
Rank: 28

When it opened in 2024, it felt like The Yellow Bittern would forever be obscured by the smog of discourse that surrounded it, concealing that, at its heart, it was a very good restaurant. 12 months and a self-imposed Instagram hiatus by its co-owner Hugh Corcoran have done the restaurant a world of good. The conspiratorial room feels lived in rather than like you’re stepping into a meme, while the set-lunch menu adds an element of mystery, demanding you surrender and put your entire trust in the proprietors. Corcoran’s food has the élan and nerve of a Panenka: braises and soups that make you wonder if cooking has been going downhill ever since the invention of frying; the sweetest Torbay prawns, served with nothing but mayonnaise; trout en papillote in a pool of butter, bay and mace. There is still a strong feeling that the Bittern’s owners are play-acting at running a restaurant, but I find this charming; we are all play-acting our way through life.

Name: The Bread of Life
Description: Rank: 27

Name: Sam Sandwiches
Description:
Rank: 26

There are many days when I wish London had something like an American diner, where the making and serving of good sandwiches is as natural as drawing breath. Then I remember we have Sam Sandwiches, an Algerian stall behind the masjid in Shepherd’s Bush Market. If you sit at the counter and watch Samir Ladoul at work, you will come away with an intimate understanding of the tiny gestures that make up line cooking. Choose one or two of chicken, lamb’s liver, kofte, fish or merguez (although I have come to the conclusion that two is a young man’s game) and they will be fried with egg and chips into one scoopable mass, with the additions of olives, harissa and mayonnaise, all cosseted by the airy half-moons of matlou bread. The result is every bit the equal of any NY deli; hefty, leavened by the bitterness of olives, the tang of harissa and the lightness of the bread itself.

Name: Dapur
Description:
Rank: 25

Conversations with Malaysian friends about the state of Malaysian food in London always lead back to Dapur, a canteen in Holborn run by Sharizah Hashim. You have to come no later than 12 – few restaurants benefit as much from the mixing and matching of dishes, and by 1.30pm so many are sold out you may as well not bother. The unsung heroes of the menu are vegetables, like squash cooked down in coconut milk until it is almost mush, as well as lesser-seen dishes from Johor – the Malay Peninsula’s southern thumb – like the pinkish ayam ros Johor, or steamed tofu dipped in egg, then deep-fried and stirred into sambal. There are great individual dishes, but nasi campur relies on creating a mixed plate that works together – concentrating on one is like describing individual brushmarks in a pointillist painting. When combined with other components – a pool of sambal, two halves of a boiled egg, coconut rice, peanuts and some crispy anchovies – eating these dishes has the same satisfaction as seeing the last piece of a particularly complex puzzle lock into place.

Name: Sabiib
Address: 139 High Street, W3 6LX and 5-6 Grand Parade, Green Lanes, N4 1JX
Description: Rank: 24

Name: Yuki Bar
Description:
Rank: 23

Around 2024, something strange happened in London Fields, which I have only seen once before (with P. Franco in Clapton around 2016–17): a restaurant instantly became an indispensable part of the hospitality ecosystem. Cosmetically, there’s nothing special about ex-Noma somm Yuki Kaneko’s bar: railway arches, natural wine, small plates, an aesthetic that stretches from London to Paris to Copenhagen. But Kaneko has created something that restaurant people have been craving – this is a wine bar that happens to serve food, and not the other way round. On any given night, you will find chefs trying to decompress post shift and soaking wine up with nimono (simmered dishes) – one of the more underrated Japanese genres. There’s a curious mix of austerity and pleasure here: where else in this one-horse town can you kill time with a boiled egg covered in sesame sauce and a shot glass martini? What Kaneko has created is not so much a wine bar as spiritually the first izakaya in the city.

Name: Gana
Address: 13–15 Village Way East, Rayners Lane HA2 7LX
Description:
Rank: 22

The Rayners Lane branch of Gana (a spin-off from the original Wembley branch) was the first place where I fell in love with Eelam Tamil food – its exuberance, its lack of concession to good taste, its casual violence on the palate. And while London’s baseline knowledge of the food of Sri Lanka has come on leaps and bounds in the last five years, helped by central London pioneers like Rambutan, Gana still more than holds its own. For one, it’s added a make-your-own-kotthu concession – a beautiful thing to have in deep Harrow – where you can customise a blend of crispy and chewy roti shreds to your taste (at Gana, language loses all meaning; I once dithered over spice levels here, and to my chagrin, they wrote ‘very mild’ on my receipt - it was still spicy). There are no subtle dishes at Gana, just a series of jabs and undercuts: an off-menu hot butter cuttlefish is, on a deep chemical level, tastier than every salt and pepper squid you’ve ever had, while the rabbit and venison fries, dense, sticky and taken to the point of jerky, represent the best subcontinental game cooking in town you’ll find outside of a JKS restaurant.

Name: Dong Yuan
Description:
Rank: 21

As HS2 moves in and the student housing blocks continue to rise, it was inevitable that Park Royal would start to see new restaurants joining the Syrian and Lebanese bakeries that give this West London industrial estate its unique character. What was never on the cards was a restaurant as assured as Dong Yuan, a tiny owner-operated Hunanese wok restaurant in what used to be a kebab shop. Chef Yaohua Cui presides over the burners here, sending out plates of vivid, bead-like green and red chillies, with meat and fish glossed with a caramelisation that only comes from phenomenally high heat. No-one has done wok-cooking to this level in London since Sirichai Kularbwong engulfed his kitchen in flame at the Leytonstone Singburi. One of the best dishes I’ve eaten all year is Cui’s winter melon, the gourd cut into translucent discs and cooked until soft, in a refreshing sauce made brackish from tiny freshwater shrimp. Like the original Singburi, I highly recommend getting the soup. And booking.

Name: Dalla
Description:
Rank: 20

Your meal at Dalla will almost certainly start with a frittatina, a discus-shaped omelette with the thinness of a British pancake, filled with something simple and glazed with balsamic. It’s the kind of dish that reminds you of restaurants in Italy where a seemingly basic meal might be so startling that you’re ready to swear on some mystical explanation, rather than what it actually is: technique, technique, technique. Chef Mitchell Damota has an almost scholarly passion for the breadth and depth of Italian food, which allows him to bypass what is trendy or what is proven to work in London and instead to concentrate on what he believes in. Look no further than a dish of passatelli – the missing link between pasta and sev – served with lentils, barely cooked lobster and its broth. It’s a dish at once homely and refined, proving not only that the two are not mutually exclusive, but also that the best cooking is often both.

Name: The Clove Club
Address: Shoreditch Town Hall, 380 Old Street, EC1V 9LT
Description:
Rank: 19

Isaac McHale’s Clove Club, located in a nook of Shoreditch Town Hall, is the last survivor of a pivotal era in London food when fine dining loosened its collar. Nearly 13 years later, the collar has been buttoned right back up and The Clove Club is a very different restaurant – almost East London’s grande dame – but the food still has the pared back minimalism that made the restaurant’s name. McHale’s childlike genius is his unashamed nostalgia, and his talent for making the most out of simple flavour combinations: raw Orkney scallop brought to earth by hazelnut and the musk of an EP’s worth of black truffle purée; the icy jolt of raw sardine, followed by the warmth of what is clearly cullen skink (a Scottish take on nigiri and miso soup); and game broth coated in the tears of 100-year-old Madeira. It feels strange to say this about a restaurant I remember feeling so new, but these dishes have become London classics, to be studied as much as enjoyed.

Name: Dilpasand
Description:
Rank: 18

Dilpasand is the most complete Pakistani restaurant in London right now. It’s not just that it has mastery of the grill, the karahi and the tandoor, when most restaurants would be content with just one, but also that the Karachi heritage of its owner, Asghar Khan, allows it to convincingly pull together the two major strands of London’s Pakistani dining: the Punjabi grillhouse and its successor, the new-wave Pashtun restaurant. But there are two Karachi homages on the menu that make Dilpasand unique. The first is the gola kebab, each the size of a snooker ball with the texture of a faggot, served on a buttery laccha paratha. The second is the Behari boti, a dry lamb curry, so smoky it feels like it’s been infused with frankincense, that comes with a blowsy roomali roti. Both are served with a puckering chutney and onions to balance out the intensity of the meat. I would sooner name a favourite limb than choose which one I prefer.

Name: Umut 2000
Address: Note: if you want to try somewhere like the old Umut, before its refurb, then try the new Umut, on Green Lanes.
Description:
Rank: 17

If I was compiling the seven wonders of London food then the lamb ribs at Umut 2000, one of the last places in Dalston that still has the close-up, elbows-in, lamb-fat-in-your-hair feel of a proper ocakbaşi, would be one of the first dishes on the list. There may be other great things on Onur Guzel’s menu – some days I might order a side of grilled liver, hearts or kidneys for health, each skewer interwoven with fat, or sometimes I might crave the simple pleasures of a yoğurtlu adana – but the ribs are non-negotiable. There are few pleasures greater than sitting near the mangal and ordering a 1.5x-portioned plate of ribs, cut across the bone to create raised dimples of meat. The bread tastes mainly of the grill and MSG, and if you don’t consider using it to rip off the crisped-up fat and make a little wrap, before stripping the bone with your teeth, then you are more immune to temptation than I am.

Name: BiBi
Description: Rank: 16

Name: Aladin Kebabish
Address: Note: if you don’t go to Kabul Sheeryakh across the street for ice cream right afterwards, you are missing one of the great London one–two punches.
Description: Rank: 15

Name: Bake Street
Description:
Rank: 14

It is impossible for this publication to be even remotely nonpartisan on the issue of Bake Street: two of our previous columnists work there, as well as, by sheer coincidence, our first ever writer. No other food establishment in London practises as many of the same virtues as we hold dear in restaurants: a relentless perfectionism, a healthy disrespect for cultural boundaries, a strong commitment to play. Sometimes I feel like it’s the only place in the city trying to encompass everything interesting about London in one place, sampling and remixing the city’s best food through citations and invites – where else could you find a burger based on the memory of an obscure 40 Maltby Street dish, or the head chef from Ikoyi making a club sandwich? Owner Feroz Gajia, Stoke Newington’s own DJ Premier, presides over an increasingly demented weekend-only menu, which veers from some of the most creative sandwiches in the city to soft serve, tacos, special drinks, and Chloe-Rose Crabtree’s American and Mexican-inspired bakes. Everything I write about London is just theory; Bake Street is the praxis.

Name: Asher’s Africana
Description: Rank: 13

Name: Al Kareem
Address: Note: do not miss Al Kareem’s drinks programme (the fridge), particularly the sweet lassi, which is as thick as an all-syrup Squishee, and the rabdi milk made with curds, condensed milk, cardamom, almond and rose. It is everything Momofuku’s cereal milk promised and failed to deliver.
Description:
Rank: 12

Pakistan is not known for its staunch tradition of vegetarianism, yet my favourite meatless dish anywhere in London might just be at Al Kareem, a Lahori sweet shop in Ilford that serves halwa puri on weekends amid an atmosphere of complete bedlam. Halwa puri is built around one of the great culinary accords: the burnt amber of semolina halwa, the earthiness of heavily spiced chana and the aniseed tang of potato curry, all bound together by the puri. Having eaten halwa puri around London, I can tell you that some of the better ones get one or two of these components right, but Al Kareem’s is the only one that nails all four, particularly the curd-topped halwa and the puri, which is thrown with flair into a sizzling vat of ghee by the puri chef, toqued up as if he’s at the Ritz. The puri is transported from the pan to the plate instantaneously, and is still cooking when you scoop up the chana. With essentially no choices on the menu, except whether to get puri or bhature (get both), Al Kareem is able to approach perfection through sheer repetition.

Name: Quality Wines
Description:
Rank: 11

When Quality Wines first opened back in 2018, there didn’t seem to be a need for it, except as a way to use up the dead space next to its older brother, The Quality Chop House. Who needed another wine bar serving up Mediterranean small plates? And yet in those seven years, under its head chef Nick Bramham, Quality Wines has gone from an afterthought to a destination in its own right. Like Hungarian screenwriter Emeric Pressburger, who had a feeling for the kind of antic Englishness that the English themselves had forgotten, Bramham has an outsider’s eye for aspects of Mediterranean culture that others miss, roving magpie-like through Italy, Spain, Greece and beyond. On spying something as homely as avgolemono on the menu, I have seen proud Greek men go from ‘Who is this μαλάκας?’ to insulting their own grandmothers to get the recipe. There is a perfectionism here for the simplest things: sometimes Bramham will put on the best sandwich you’ve ever eaten, as a flex, only to take it off the menu the next week.

Name: Ikoyi
Description:
Rank: 10

When Jeremy Chan and Iré Hassan-Odukale opened Ikoyi in St James in 2017, they managed to kid themselves – or kid their PR – that they were opening a West African restaurant. Now that it’s on the Strand and no longer serving pink-glitter plantains, it has given up the pretence of being tied to any one region of Earth. Instead, it showcases Chan’s Martian cuisine – galactic black plectrums of dried citrus, squid chewed up and repurposed as marshmallow – equal parts menacing and beautiful.

The best of Chan’s food, particularly the self-contained smaller dishes that come earlier in the menu, has the quality of great perfumery – in that he is able, through the accretion of tiny, molecular details, to create new contours of flavour. Where Ikoyi differs from its competition is its almost-reckless use of titanic ingredients (long pepper, aged meat, saffron, chilli), balanced across multiple axes in an attempt to create something daintier than the sum of its many parts. Of course, the £350 question is whether Ikoyi is worth this kind of money. What meal can be? But if you have the cash and you want to try the pinnacle of this kind of virtuosic cooking, then you won’t find a better version in London.

Name: Kaieteur Kitchen Original
Address: Note: Kaieteur Kitchen is currently closed due to a dispute with its landlord, but you can find Faye cooking at Walworth Living Room on Fridays, including tonight. It remains on this list in the knowledge that form is temporary but class is permanent.
Description:
Rank: 9

One measure of greatness is the highest level someone is capable of achieving. Another, which the goalkeeper Peter Schmeichel once used to discuss the greatness of Paul Scholes, is when a person’s ‘bottom level’, their worst performance, is so high that it barely registers. Using this metric, Faye Gomes, who is incapable of cooking a dish that isn’t at least an 8/10, is one of the greatest chefs in the city. When her Guyanese food business Kaieteur Kitchen moved from being a one-woman takeaway to a restaurant, you might have feared a slip of quality control, but instead the food is somehow even better. It’s the cooking of someone who is not looking to impress, or to impose their will, but to feed – with all the holistic qualities that entails. Most people don’t bother ordering and just leave it to Gomes to choose what’s good: fried fish, spiced pumpkin, spinach rice, roti – things you’d be happy eating everyday for the rest of your life. The pepper pot on Friday, however, is a once–a-year treat: meat and cow’s foot cooked down with orange peel and thyme for two days until it’s the colour of vinyl, with a phenomenal bittersweetness that comes from cassareep, a thick treacle made from cassava root.

If you told me you’d had a bad meal at any of the other restaurants on this list – even great ones higher up – I would commiserate and accept that they’d had an off day. If you told me you had a bad meal at Kaieteur Kitchen, I would simply shake your hand and tell you that I can’t help you.

Name: St. John Bread and Wine
Description: Rank: 8

Name: Charsi Karahi
Description:
Rank: 7

Every time I eat at Charsi Karahi, Atiulla Safi’s Afghan restaurant opposite Norbury station, it feels electric, a reminder of the force with which Pashtun cooking has reshaped London’s South Asian dining scene. Along with its Pakistani cousins Taste of Pakistan and Namak Mandi, Charsi Karahi has taught Londoners to wait, pioneering a fresh, ‘let’s-do-it-live’ approach to karahi cooking that relies on building curries and reducing them down with extreme heat to order. What sets Charsi apart is its consistency across the Pashtun repertoire – the tanginess of its karahis, the wreta kebabs, arranged around a central dais of bone marrow, the muscularity of its grill cooking. I often suspect it is the best meat specialist in the city.

This is without even getting into its hero dish, which is a whole lamb. An unfeasible number of South London parties, weddings and funerals have been catered with this lamb (including my own birthday). Pre-ordering it necessitates making it an event: 30 stout eaters, floor seats composed around a green tarpaulin to protect the carpet, and enough room to stretch out and lie down afterwards. The lamb itself is really a very expensive container for the plump, glossy rice, steamed inside the animal’s belly. One type of person would make a beeline for the most prized cuts of meat and add them to their Kabuli pulao; a wiser one would crack open the ribcage, find the rice and squeeze cooked garlic cloves over it like chip shop sachets of mayonnaise.

Name: Bouchon Racine
Description:
Rank: 6

If Bouchon Racine is the first, best and most consistent restaurant of London’s improbable post-Brexit French resurgence, perhaps it’s because it was never a reaction to something in the air, but rather the second coming of chef Henry Harris’s much-missed Racine, reimagined in an intimate townhouse in Farringdon.
